title: Use equivalent fractions to solve sharing, measuring and recipe problems

lesson.title: Equivalent Fractions in Real Life

steps.say: You already know how to check if two fractions are equivalent, like three quarters and six eighths. Today we use that skill for something handy: solving real sharing, measuring, and recipe problems.

visual.caption: Three quarters and six eighths cover the same amount

steps.say: Here is the big idea. When the whole stays the same, you can cut it into more, smaller pieces and still have exactly the same amount. Look at the two bars. The top bar is cut into four pieces with three shaded. The bottom bar is cut into eight pieces with six shaded. The shaded parts line up perfectly. So if a recipe asks for three quarters, six eighths works just as well.

visual.caption: Same whole, smaller pieces, same amount

steps.say: Let's try a real one. You are baking banana muffins in Vancouver, and the recipe needs three quarters of a cup of oats. But the only scoop you can find is a one eighth cup scoop. How many scoops do you need? Change three quarters into eighths. Multiply the top and the bottom by two: three times two is six, and four times two is eight. So three quarters equals six eighths. You need six scoops of the little one eighth cup.

visual.caption: Six scoops of one eighth of a cup

steps.say: Now here is a mistake I see all the time. Someone says, one half is bigger than one quarter, so one half of the small chocolate bar must be more than one quarter of the big bar. Let's check with real numbers. The big bar is forty centimetres long, so one quarter of it is ten centimetres. The small bar is only ten centimetres long, so one half of it is five centimetres. Ten centimetres beats five centimetres! Fractions only tell the whole story when the wholes are the same size. Always ask yourself first: one quarter of what?

labels: One quarter of the big bar
One half of the small bar
visual.caption: Different wholes, so you must compare the real amounts

steps.say: So when a recipe or a measuring problem gives you pieces of a different size, don't panic. Rename the fraction so its bottom number matches the size of the pieces you actually have, and count them up.
steps.headline: Rename the bottom to match the pieces you have

lesson.answer: Rename the fraction to match the pieces you have — and only compare fractions when the wholes are the same size.

practice.question: You are making pancakes and the recipe needs two thirds of a cup of milk. The only scoop in the drawer holds one sixth of a cup. How many scoops of milk do you need? Hint: draw a bar cut into three pieces with two shaded, then cut every piece in half.
practice.answer: 4 scoops. Two thirds equals four sixths, because two times two is four and three times two is six.
